How the world uses AI — a guide to the data

Diversity in a Globalized World

Published

September 9, 2026

What this data is about

Most research on AI and work asks a question it cannot really answer: which jobs could a machine do? People build lists of tasks, judge how automatable each one looks, and add them up. It is a reasonable exercise, but it is a prediction about the future, not a record of anything that happened.

This data is different. It is a record of what people actually did.

Anthropic, the company that makes the AI assistant Claude, took millions of real conversations, stripped out anything identifying, and classified each one: what kind of work was it, what occupation does that work belong to, was the person studying or working or doing something personal. Then they published the totals, country by country.

So instead of “jobs like this could be automated”, you get “in Tunisia, half of what people ask Claude for is coursework.”

This folder contains that data for 121 countries, ready to map.

The two files

File Use it for What one row is
countries.rds Maps One country
occupations.rds Comparing what countries use AI for One country, one occupation group 
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

countries   <- readRDS("preprocessed_data/countries.rds")
occupations <- readRDS("preprocessed_data/occupations.rds")

countries.rds — for maps

One row per country, with the shape of the country attached.

Variable What it means
iso3 Three-letter country code
country Country name
continent Continent
adoption_rate How much this country uses Claude, relative to its size
used_for_work % of conversations that are work
used_for_study % that are coursework or studying
used_for_personal % that are personal
automation_style % where the person handed over a whole task
augmentation_style % where the person worked with the AI rather than delegating
asked_to_explain % where the person wanted the AI to teach them something
asked_to_just_do_it % where the person gave an instruction and wanted output
geometry The country’s shape — you never touch this directly

A map takes one line:

ggplot(countries) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = used_for_study), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "rocket", direction = -1, na.value = "grey93",
                       name = "% of use") +
  labs(title = "Where AI is used for studying") +
  coord_sf(crs = "+proj=robin") +
  theme_void()

Swap used_for_study for any other variable and you get a different map.

There are 241 shapes but only 121 countries have data. The rest come out grey. That is not a mistake — Claude is not used everywhere, and the grey is itself information.

Variable What it means
iso3, country, continent Same as above
occupation One of 22 occupation groups
pct % of that country’s AI use falling in this group

Each country’s percentages add to roughly 100.

The thing worth noticing first

The occupational mix barely changes from country to country. Computing is around a quarter of use almost everywhere; teaching around a seventh. Wherever you look, people use AI for similar kinds of work.

But the purpose changes enormously.

countries |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(iso3 %in% c("TUN","IDN","COL","MEX","BRA","DEU","USA")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(country, used_for_study), y = used_for_study)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#b44527", width = 0.6) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Share of AI use that is coursework",
       x = NULL, y = "% of conversations") +
  theme_minimal()

In Tunisia over half of all use is studying. In the United States it is under one in ten, and personal use is nearly half. Mexico sits at about 21%.

Same tool, available on the same terms everywhere, absorbed into completely different parts of life. That is the most interesting thing in this data, and it is a question about societies rather than about technology.

The big limitation — read this before you conclude anything

This measures the people who use Claude, not the people who live in a country.

Look at adoption_rate: the United States is around 20, Tunisia around 0.3. So “half of Tunisian use is coursework” means half of a small group — almost certainly younger, more urban, better connected and more educated than Tunisians in general.

That does not make the number wrong. It makes it a statement about a particular group of people, and you have to say so. Compare that with the China Shock data, where the denominator is every worker in a place.

Whenever you write a sentence beginning “in country X, people…”, stop and ask whether you mean people or Claude users. Almost always you mean the second.

Other things worth knowing

automation_style and augmentation_style add to 100. They split every conversation into two kinds: handing over a whole task, or working alongside the AI. Mapping either one shows where AI is a delegate and where it is a collaborator.

adoption_rate is extremely lopsided. A few countries are very high and most are near zero. On a plain map almost everything looks the same — try trans = "sqrt" inside scale_fill_viridis_c().

The data covers May 2026, one month. It is a snapshot, not a trend.

Questions you could ask

  • Which countries use AI mostly for study, and what do they have in common?
  • Is used_for_study related to how rich a country is, or how young it is? You would need to bring in outside data to check.
  • Does automation_style differ between richer and poorer countries — do some places delegate to AI while others collaborate with it?
  • Do countries with high adoption_rate use AI differently from countries just starting out?
  • Take one continent. Are neighbouring countries similar, or not at all?
  • Where does Mexico sit, and which countries is it most like?

Where the data comes from

The Anthropic Economic Index, release of 26 June 2026, published under a CC-BY licence at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Anthropic/EconomicIndex.

Country outlines come from Natural Earth. We took the country-level tables from the June 2026 release, kept the May 2026 month, renamed the variables into plain English and attached the map shapes.
